summary:
Curaçao is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, with full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is legal, with an equal age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. A trans visitor in a relationship read locally as same-sex faces no conduct offence on that basis.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Curaçao since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld an Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Before that ruling, Curaçao recognised as valid same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, but offered no in-island marriage, civil union or other form of recognition.

Recognition arrived by court order rather than by statute. A limited-rights proposal was put to the Estates of Curaçao in 2017, and a marriage bill submitted on 4 June 2019 was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support. In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights quickly, and the August 2015 Oliari and Others v. Italy judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, applicable to Curaçao, required legal recognition.

The Criminal Code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds that include heterosexual or homosexual orientation. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any distinction affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights in political, economic, social, cultural or other social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The protected grounds named in the source material do not include gender identity, and no Curaçao-specific authority on gender-identity coverage was identified.

Official rhetoric has not consistently governed practice. In April 2015 commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly backed equal rights for everyone in the local press, while her party colleague Winifred Raveneau opposed the rights push fiercely and used a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement to force Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel premises. Public LGBT assembly on the island can be obstructed through administrative permitting at short notice.

Curaçao opened an LGBT community centre, the Pink House, in 2010, and alongside Aruba and Sint Maarten has acted as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay welcoming in the region, and a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

No Curaçao-specific sourcing was found on gender markers in locally issued identity documents, entry or border screening triggered by gender presentation, access to gender-affirming care, or the designation of facilities. Those areas are unassessed rather than cleared.
tangentialFactors:
Aruba, a separate constituent country in the same Kingdom, passed same-sex civil partnerships on 8 September 2016. That is comparator context and not Curaçao law.

The April 2015 agreement covered Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten jointly, so the direction of travel was Kingdom-wide rather than specific to Curaçao.

The IGLTA award cited by Curaçao Gay Pride is a promotional characterisation by a local organiser, not an independent assessment of conditions for trans visitors.
localsOnly:
Recognition of same-sex marriage in Curaçao rests on the 12 July 2024 ruling of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands rather than on an act of the Estates; the 2017 limited-rights proposal and the 2019 marriage bill withdrawn in September 2020 both failed in the legislature.

The Criminal Code's discrimination provisions name heterosexual or homosexual orientation as protected grounds and do not name gender identity, so a resident seeking to bring a discrimination complaint on gender-identity grounds has no provision identified in the source material.

Local organisers face administrative permitting as a practical constraint: the 2013 Gay Pride was forced to relocate to a hotel premises by a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement.

The Pink House, opened in 2010, is the island's LGBT community centre.
outOfScopeNotes:
Gender markers in locally issued identity documents, entry and border screening triggered by gender presentation, access to gender-affirming care, and facility designation are unassessed for Curaçao; no region-specific sourcing was identified.

Whether the Criminal Code's discrimination provisions have been applied to gender-identity complaints is not sourced.

The IGLTA award and the delivery of a rights wishes-package to ministers in The Hague are recorded as claims by the organisations involved; no outcome from the wishes-package is documented in the source material.
